title: Book of Rites — the Chinese text
dateDisplay: Compiled 1st century BCE from earlier material
attributionNote: Compiled in the Han dynasty, traditionally by Dai Sheng (fl. 1st century BCE), from ritual writings of several earlier centuries and hands; no single author can be named for the collection.
description: The Liji is the prose heart of the Confucian ritual tradition: chapters on sacrifice and mourning, the ordering of the household and the state, the duties of the scholar and the meaning of music. Two of its chapters, the Great Learning and the Mean, were later lifted out and made books of the Four Books, and its picture of the 'Great Unity' remains one of the most quoted passages in Chinese political thought.
historicalContext: The collection took shape as the ritual canon of the Han: Dai Sheng's recension of the older records displaced the longer Da Dai Liji and became the text read with the Zhouli and Yili as the Three Rites. The chapters differ widely in date and doctrine. This record is the Chinese text alone.
availabilityNote: Complete in the Chinese Text Project's transcription: 38 chapters as the site divides it, 1,761 paragraphs, streamed from ctext.org one chapter at a time. This is the original Chinese, not a translation. When the site cannot be read, the chapter is served from the library's validated import cache.
